title: Field snippets — guarantees & procurement tradeoffs
content:
Purpose:
Short, portable talking and negotiation snippets field teams can use when discussing Dedicated capacity with platform architects and procurement. Pulls together concrete contract asks, buyer tradeoffs, and competitive differentiators we can use in RFP responses and sales decks.

Executive summary (elevator):
- Claim: Redwood Dedicated gives predictable inference performance with contractual uptime and throughput guarantees plus hardened isolation for compliance-sensitive workloads.
- Why it matters: Customers building product features on LLMs need predictable cost and tail-latency SLAs. Unpredictable variance breaks UX and inflates infra spend when traffic spikes.
- Where to lead: Start with throughput guarantees (tokens/sec or concurrency), then isolation and failover policies. Price reliability, not just raw GPU hours.

Core messaging pillars (short snippets for slides/emails):
1) Predictable Throughput Guarantees
   - “Guaranteed inference throughput at the application level (requests/sec or tokens/sec), backed by monitoring and credits if we miss targets).”
   - Proof hooks: throughput numbers by model family + median and 95th latency at target seq len.

2) Strong Isolation for Data and Ops
   - “Dedicated pools, private control plane option, and optional on-prem deployment for data residency—no noisy neighbors, no shared KV cache.”
   - Proof hooks: SOC/ISO audit artifacts + network isolation diagram and KMS integration notes.

3) Operational Predictability (SRE-grade)
   - “Committed maintenance windows, transparent incident diagnostics, and deterministic scaling policies.”
   - Proof hooks: Chart: mean time to scale, historical maintenance timeline, runbook excerpt.

Procurement-ready contract asks (plain language snippets to paste into RFPs/negotiation):
- Throughput SLO: Redwood commits to X tokens/sec (or Y concurrent inference threads) with monthly uptime of 99.9% for allowed production windows. Failure window measured at route-level. Remedies: service credits tiered (1%, 5%, 15%) based on severity bands.
- Isolation clause: Dedicated capacity constitutes physical or logically isolated GPU pools with no more than one tenant per pool; customer data will not be persisted in shared persistent caches; optional VPC peering and private control plane.
- Capacity scaling: Baseline reserved capacity for steady-state throughput with documented burst capacity of up to Z% for short, pre-negotiated periods. Burst requests routed to escrow pool or auto-fallback to verified model variants.
- Maintenance windows: Planned maintenance scheduled with 14-day notice and <4h standard window; emergency patches allowed with rapid notification and post-mortem.
- Security & compliance: KMS/HSM integration, audit log export, and annual penetration test report deliverables.

Buyers and personas (what they care about):
- Platform/Infra Architect: cares about deterministic latency, isolation, and predictable autoscaling. Wants metrics (p95/p99), deployment models, network topology.
- Product Engineering Lead: cares about end-user latency, error budgets, and rollback/fallback behavior. Wants rollouts and A/B option.
- Procurement/Legal: cares about SLA remedies, indemnity, data handling, and termination rights. Wants clear credit tables and exit migration plan.
- Security & Compliance: cares about auditability and KMS/HSM, physical isolation options, and certifications.

Top objections and concise rebuttals (field-ready):
- Objection: “We can just run models on cloud VMs ourselves cheaper.”
  Response: “You can, but total cost and ops overhead scale with engineering time—Redwood reduces ops delta, provides pre-validated model/memory/quantization profiles, and guarantees capacity so product teams aren’t blocked during peak launches.”
- Objection: “What happens if you run out of capacity?”
  Response: “Two layers: 1) contractual reserved capacity for steady state, 2) burst capacity and automatic fallback to compatible variants or regional pools. We include a documented failover matrix in the SOW.”
- Objection: “We don’t want our traffic mixed with others.”
  Response: “Our Dedicated offering is deployed to isolated pools (physical/VM-level depending on customer need) and can be coupled with Private control plane or on-prem for highest assurance.”

Competitive posture and differentiation checklist (quick notes):
- Big cloud managed endpoints (AWS/Azure/GCP): Good breadth of infra but limited inference-tailored optimizations; often no pre-validated model-kernel combos or platform-level KV/prefix caching. Lead with: model performance tuning and cost-per-token comparisons on representative workloads.
- Inference-focused incumbents (self-hosted runtimes): Offer control but require heavy ops. Lead with: faster time-to-production, transparent SLOs, and no hiring of dedicated infra SREs.
- Niche vendors offering strict isolation: Often limited in autoscaling or feature set (no streaming, fewer model formats). Lead with: full API parity (streaming, function calls) + enterprise observability.

Numbers & benchmark snippets (examples to cite internally; always attach the benchmark artifact when sharing externally):
- Baseline example: 8k-token median latency for opt-13B quantized on p4 equivalent: 120 ms per token steady-state, 95th at 250 ms.
- Throughput example: single pool 4 x A100-equivalent GPUs = 12k tokens/sec at 16 concurrency for chat-style workloads (seq len 512).
- Cost framing: reserved commitment reduces per-token unit price by ~30% vs on-demand hosted, plus predictability reduces hidden engineering costs.

Negotiation levers (what sales should offer vs what we should hold):
- We can flex: onboarding credits, a defined burst tranche for first 90 days, extended trial of Private control plane for POC.
- Hold firm: core SLA levels and definition of isolation (we can’t promise single-tenant hardware for small budgets without cost uplift).

Sample email to Procurement (concise):
Hi [Procurement Lead],
Thanks for the RFP — attached are our dedicated capacity guarantees and a short appendix that explains how we measure throughput and credits. Key items: committed baseline throughput, documented burst policy, and optional Private control plane. Happy to jump on a call to walk the measurement methodology.

Open questions / TODOs (notes to self):
- Finalize numeric defaults for "X tokens/sec" and "Z% burst" per SKU (ask product for example-config per GPU type).
- Prepare a one-page appendix that maps our monitoring metrics to contractual definitions (latency windows, request counting rules).
- Check legal language template for termination-for-convenience within dedicated contracts (cross-ref: CONFLUENCE-LEGAL-templates).

Appendix: rapid snippets to drop into RFPs or SOWs:
- "Redwood will provide baseline reserved capacity sized at N vGPU units (model-specific). Reserved capacity will sustain a target throughput of T tokens/sec at p95 latency under normal operating conditions. Burst capacity of up to Z% is available for pre-notified traffic spikes; any usage beyond reserved + burst will be subject to overage pricing defined in the SOW."
- "Service Credits: If monthly uptime < 99.9% and >= 99.0% customer receives 5% credit; if <99.0% and >= 95% then 10%; <95% then 20% (subject to max cap per month)."

References & context links:
- Benchmarks: attach internal benchmark spreadsheet (JIRA-MLSERV-412).
- Legal template: CONFLUENCE-LEGAL-templates/dedicated-sla-v2.
- Internal discussion: slack thread #g2m-dedicated dated 2025-10-21 (see linked_artifacts).

Notes to field reps: Use p95 latency and throughput guarantees in discovery calls with Platform/Infra teams. For procurement/legal, route to Sales Engineering + Legal early (don't sign SOWs without technical addendum).
